builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: A Differential Computing Accelerator for LLM Inference Leveraging Bit-Slice Transition Sparsity
summary: The method replaces standard bit-slice GEMM datapaths with a Steiner-point reuse scheme in which partial sums of clustered bit-slice vectors are reconstructed from shared representative patterns via a few additions or subtractions, implemented as a custom algorithm-hardware co-designed accelerator. Adoption requires fabricating or licensing new silicon, including the SATC table construction, FlipPrune preprocessing for weights, and dedicated on-chip logic for runtime K/V handling; none of this is implementable on a single GPU or through an API. The approach can fail in practice if BSV clustering is weaker on real model distributions than assumed, if FlipPrune degrades model accuracy, or if the speedups measured against other research accelerators do not translate to mainstream GPU-based deployment.
rationale: The technique is a custom hardware accelerator design evaluated only against other research ASICs, so it offers no adoptable software or method for an engineer limited to a 24 GB GPU or third-party APIs.

claims.statement: The method replaces standard bit-slice GEMM datapaths with a Steiner-point reuse scheme in which partial sums of clustered bit-slice vectors are reconstructed from shared representative patterns via a few additions or subtractions, implemented as a custom algorithm-hardware co-designed accelerator. Adoption requires fabricating or licensing new silicon, including the SATC table construction, FlipPrune preprocessing for weights, and dedicated on-chip logic for runtime K/V handling; none of this is implementable on a single GPU or through an API. The approach can fail in practice if BSV clustering is weaker on real model distributions than assumed, if FlipPrune degrades model accuracy, or if the speedups measured against other research accelerators do not translate to mainstream GPU-based deployment.

Reported average speedups of 3.09x, 2.41x, 2.18x, 1.27x, and 1.41x over the specialized accelerators ANT, BBS, LUT Tensor Core, Transitive Array, and MCBP-BRCR, respectively; no comparison to commodity GPUs or CPUs.
